title: Western Ghats Lit Fest 2026 | Day 2: Speakers explore Bharat’s civilisational heritage and challenges
excerpt: Coimbatore: The second day of the fifth edition of the Western Ghats Lit Fest 2026, held on October 25, witnessed discussions on the status of Hindus in Bharat, religious discrimination, temple administration, India’s maritime heritage, national security, economic thought, inner science and the country’s civilisational legacy. Speakers also examined ideological narratives, the Naxal movement, cow protection and the importance of preserving India’s cultural and literary traditions. The day began with prayers and the lighting of the ceremonial lamp, followed by an invocation by Sree Raja Durga. Anand Ranganathan questions discrimination against Hindus In his keynote address on Status of Hindus in the State of Bharat, author and commentator Dr Anand Ranganathan spoke about what he described as discrimination against Hindus, unequal treatment of religious institutions and the need for a change in policy. He said, “It is not a question of being second-class or third-class citizens. I thought things would possibly get better in the years to come. I am afraid that things have either got worse or remained the same. The Hindu candle, metaphorically speaking, is burning at both ends. If it were burning at only one end, we could possibly manage the situation or salvage something for a few more years. But the problem is that it is burning at both ends.” He argued that appeasement was being extended to all communities except Hindus and that differential treatment existed even within the Hindu community. He said the problem arose when appeasement crossed the boundary into discrimination. Referring to religious conversions, he said conversions through coercion, force or inducement were a different matter. Ranganathan also questioned what he described as a new phenomenon of Hindus celebrating conversions away from Hinduism. He said there was no objection to individuals choosing another religion, but questioned the attitude of those celebrating the departure of others from their religious tradition. He referred to instances of political leaders celebrating such conversions. Government control of Hindu temples Questioning the state control of Hindu temples, Ranganathan asked why Hindu temples alone were subjected to government control while mosques and gurdwaras were not governed by comparable arrangements. He questioned why a practice inherited from the British period continued after Independence and why the relevant constitutional and legal concerns had been overlooked when the Congress government introduced endowment laws in the 1950s. He said thousands of Hindu temples had subsequently come under government control. According to him, more than one lakh Hindu temples were under government control, leaving their administration vulnerable to the decisions of those in power. He alleged that temple funds could be diverted, temple lands taken over and institutions that had sustained Hindu religious and cultural life for centuries placed at the mercy of governments. Also Read: Western Ghats Lit Fest 2026 | Day 1: National security, heritage, Indic knowledge and Hindu identity take centre stage He cited Tamil Nadu as an example, stating that nearly 40,000 temples were under government control. Karnataka had a comparable number, approximately 35,000 to 36,000, he said. In Andhra Pradesh, he referred to laws and administrative practices that imposed financial obligations on prominent temples, including Tirupati. He questioned the practice of directing temple funds towards government projects such as flyovers and meeting administrative expenses, including audits. Referring to Keralam, he said the Communist establishment, despite describing religion as the opium of the masses, had exercised control over thousands of temples through various boards. He also referred to the difficulties faced by Sabarimala pilgrims, alleging that devotees had been packed together like sardines, with some reportedly suffocating and dying. Agama temples and Tamil Nadu’s temple administration Ranganathan criticised the Tamil Nadu government’s move concerning the classification of Agama temples as non-Agama temples. He referred to the figure of 30,000 out of the 40,000 temples under the Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments (HR&CE) Department. He described the development as disastrous, arguing that Agama temples had functioned according to established traditions for centuries, with priests performing specific duties passed down through generations. He said, “Suddenly, an administrator arrives and declares that the temple is no longer an Agama temple. According to the figures I have cited, this has happened to 25,000 temples.” He alleged that decisions detrimental to Hindu interests taken by the previous DMK government were being continued by the present government. Referring to the Thiruparankundram Karthigai Deepam issue, he said the TVK government had approached the Supreme Court in the matter and had not withdrawn its position despite judicial criticism of the earlier government’s actions. He also referred to the parole granted to individuals convicted in connection with the Coimbatore bombings, despite the Supreme Court having indicated that bail should be denied to them. He said parole had been granted to five associates of the mastermind Basha, who died approximately a year earlier. He also criticised the permission given for a procession through the same roads during Basha’s funeral, which drew thousands of Muslims. ‘Apply the same rules to mosques and churches’ Arguing that Hindus needed to recalibrate their demands, Ranganathan said that if the government maintained that existing laws governing Hindu institutions were not discriminatory, comparable rules should be applied to other religious institutions. He said Hindus should stop merely asking the state to relinquish control over temples and instead demand that the state take control of mosques and churches as well. “If the state can interfere in one community’s religious institutions, why should it not interfere in those belonging to other communities?” he asked, arguing that the government would probably relinquish control over Hindu temples within 24 hours if such a demand were made. He questioned the logic of government takeovers in the name of preventing corruption, asking whether corruption in any organisation justified its takeover by the state. He also questioned how a government frequently accused of corruption could be considered the appropriate institution to eliminate corruption in religious bodies. He said the Congress was responsible for introducing several of the laws, but questioned why the present government continued to implement them. Places of Worship Act and […]

title: Karnataka tech funding jumps 26% to $4.6 billion even as funding rounds plunge 35%
excerpt: Technology companies in Karnataka raised $4.6 billion in the first nine months of 2026, 26% more than the $3.7 billion they raised a year earlier, even as the number of funding rounds fell 35% to 397, according to market intelligence platform Tracxn. Almost every dollar of it went to one city. The figures come from Tracxn's Karnataka Tech 9M 2026 report, which covers equity funding, investors, exits and unicorns in the state between 1 January and 30 September 2026. It follows the firm's India Tech report in September, which put national tech funding at $10.3 billion for a similar stretch, a rise of 7%. "9M 2026 remains at 30% of the funding peak of $15.4B reached in 9M 2021," the report said. Karnataka's startups raised $15.4 billion in the first nine months of 2021, at the height of the pandemic-era funding boom. The current total is also only 5% above the $4.4 billion raised in the same period of 2024, so the 26% jump is a recovery from a weak 2025 rather than a return to the old numbers. Fewer rounds, much bigger cheques The round count tells the opposite story to the dollar count. At 397, it is down 35% from 610 in 9M 2025 and 42% from 681 in 9M 2024. Work the two numbers against each other and the average round in Karnataka comes to roughly $11.6 million, against about $6.1 million a year earlier. Concentration explains most of the rise. The ten largest rounds together raised $2.0 billion, about 44% of all the money. CRED's $540 million Series H in June, which the report says was backed by Meta, was alone equal to about 12% of the state's total. Rounds at Series A and beyond fell only 6%, to 166 from 176. So the collapse in deal count sits almost entirely in the small rounds below that line. The rounds that moved the number After CRED came Sarvam, the Bengaluru startup building a generative AI platform for enterprises and governments, which raised $255 million in a Series B in June backed by HCL Technologies, Bessemer Venture Partners and Peak XV Partners, and another $90 million in August with Nvidia among the investors. Ride-hailing platform Rapido raised $240 million in a Series F in May from Prosus, WestBridge Capital and Accel. Digital lender KreditBee raised $220 million in a Series E in April, led by investors including Motilal Oswal. Fintech and enterprise applications were the top-funded sectors at $1.4 billion each, up 44% and 37% respectively. The sharpest move was in auto tech, at $896 million, up 420% from $172 million a year earlier. Electric two-wheeler maker Simple Energy's $180 million Series C in September, Rideriver's $102 million and Ultraviolette's $85 million sit behind that jump. Where the squeeze shows Seed funding fell to $281 million, down 32% from $412 million in 9M 2025 and 39% from $458 million in 9M 2024. Seed rounds made up 58% of all deals but only 6% of the money. Late-stage rounds were 9% of deals and 57% of the money. The number of companies raising institutional money for the first time fell 45%, to 86 from 155. Investors thinned out too. The report counted 264 existing institutional investors in the state, down 25% from 350, while first-time investors rose 10% to 102. Antler was the most active seed investor with 10 investments, and Peak XV Partners the most active early-stage investor with nine. The national picture is the same shape. India's seed funding fell 37% to $698 million in the period and first-time funded companies dropped 30% to 338, even as total funding rose. Three unicorns, reached much faster Karnataka produced three unicorns, companies valued at $1 billion or more, the same as last year: Emergent, Sarvam and KreditBee. What changed is the speed. The average time from a Series A round to the round that took a company past $1 billion was 1.7 years, against 8.8 years in 9M 2025, and the average funding raised before that round was $130 million. Emergent, a startup building a platform that creates full-stack applications using AI, crossed the mark in July, 0.9 years after its Series A and with $100 million raised before its unicorn round. Across India, six startups turned unicorn in the period, taking 4.9 years on average from Series A, according to Tracxn's national report. Acquisitions halved, listings held up Karnataka tech companies saw 20 acquisitions, down 49% from 39 a year earlier, at an average disclosed price of $55 million. The largest was upGrad's purchase of edtech company Unacademy at $222 million. Unacademy had raised $880 million before the sale, so the price works out to about a quarter of the money investors had put in. Marico bought skincare brand Cosmix for $25 million and Meesho bought retailer network app Kirana Club for $21 million. Four companies listed, against three a year earlier, but at an average market value of $522 million on listing day, down from $961 million. Cloud media technology company Amagi led at $858 million, followed by logistics firm Shadowfax at $782 million and rental platform Rentomojo at $438 million. Both January listings began badly and have since moved well past their offer prices. Amagi sold shares at Rs 361 and closed at Rs 547.05 on the BSE on Monday. Shadowfax, which priced its issue at Rs 124, closed at Rs 272.40. Everything outside Bengaluru is a rounding error "Bengaluru, Mysuru and Shivamogga were the top 3 funded cities in 9M 2026, together accounting for 100% of all funding raised," the report said. In practice the list is one city. Bengaluru's share of state funding was 100%, as it was in 9M 2025. Mysuru came second with $8 million, almost all of it from quick-commerce startup BazaarNow. Shivamogga recorded $154,000, Belgaum $107,000 and Mangaluru $81,000. Bengaluru has absorbed $87.1 billion of the $87.3 billion raised by Karnataka tech companies since the data intelligence began tracking them.

title: Western Ghats Lit Fest 2026 | Day 1: National security, heritage, Indic knowledge and Hindu identity take centre stage
excerpt: The fifth edition of the Western Ghats Lit Fest, held in Coimbatore on October 24 and 25 witnessed the participation of the Tamil Nadu Governor, army veterans, authors, students and eminent personalities who make it a point never to miss the event. Defence and national security On the first day, the session began with the lighting of the ceremonial lamp, pooja and prayers by Sivakumar Shivachariayar, followed by an invocation song by Sree Raja Durga. In his keynote address, author Nitin Gokhale spoke on Restraint to Response – India’s New Security Doctrine in detail. He said, “My group is called Bharat Shakti. It was deliberately chosen. We wanted, and still want, to support India’s quest for Atmanirbhar or self-reliance in the defence sector and other critical and deep technologies. And that is why the name was chosen very deliberately. I could have easily called it India’s Defence Review, Strategic or whatever, but I chose to name it Bharat Shakti, and now it has caught on. A lot of people talk about Bharat and Bharat Shakti and strength. It is particularly useful for students to know how national security is handled as far as the Indian national structure is concerned.” Explaining further, he recalled that earlier India used to adopt restraint when provoked, irrespective of the magnitude of the provocation. India was very hesitant in taking action or responding to terrorist attacks or similar incidents. We can look at the period after 1998, particularly the first 15–16 years of this century. Read More: Theyyam – Centuries old tradition of Malabar: A stage where divinity meets humanity For years, India felt like, or acted like, a boxer who would not punch back when Pakistan attacked J&K or other cities. Coimbatore itself has suffered. We are aware of the bomb blasts that happened here, in which Advani, the Union Home Minister at that time, was the target. There was no pushback from India. We were just absorbing the punches, especially from Pakistan. China was still very dominant at that point. Gokhale said, “All the insurgencies, terror attacks and violence were happening across the country, including Punjab, Mumbai, Delhi, Varanasi, Bengaluru, Pune, Guwahati and Jammu and Kashmir. Every place had suffered a bomb blast or a terrorist attack. “When the Mumbai attacks took place in November 2008, in which 175 were killed and several hundred injured, they went unanswered. Former NSA Shivshankar Menon is on record in his book that there was a discussion in the government at that time, when UPA-I was in power, about what action, including kinetic or military action, should be taken against Pakistan. Most people preferred that no action was needed. The then Prime Minister finally acceded to that. “It emboldened Pakistan further because no cost was imposed. This attitude made Pakistan more and more brazen and bold in spreading attacks across the country. There was a hesitation, as if terrorist attacks and violence by terrorists were inevitable. I personally reported all this from the front lines…” He said China was a difficult challenge to handle, given its military might and wealth. Its economy was five times larger than India’s, and it remained India’s primary adversary. There were peace talks. Cheap and poor-quality Chinese goods flooded Indian markets, forcing many businesses to shut down. Many became bankrupt. Pakistan was a subset of the China challenge. After 2014, things started changing. The police and defence sectors were given a free hand to handle any eventualities in their own way. There were no impediments. Now, the message is clear: retaliation is certain and will be on a bigger scale. There is no longer a policy of taking things lightly and forgetting them. In the past, India followed a multi-aligned or multipolar approach, as opposed to non-alignment. Now, India is proactive. The NSA now has two deputies. They have more powers and can generate Cabinet notes, access Cabinet papers and convene inter-ministerial meetings. Under Prime Minister Narendra Modi, the foreign policy and security sectors have become proactive, pragmatic and bold, with seamless security coordination. In tune with modern-day technologies, the defence sector is adopting AI, quantum computing and other advanced technologies. Major General (Retd) Bipin Bakshi, in his address on Conventional Battlefield and the Hybrid Battlespace, dwelt at length on the differences between conventional and modern tactics. He said countries were facing more proxy wars through modern-day technological inventions. Until 2025, there had been no Indian response to various terror attacks in India. Through Operation Sindoor, India had proved its strength and tactics to the world and issued a strong warning about what would happen if anyone attacked India. He said a Pakistani minister had described it as the “dirty work of the USA” after the Pahalgam attack. The Mujahideen were created with Sudanese and Afghan elements to help Pakistan. They were trained in terror-linked activities. It was originally intended to take on Russia. They later tried their hand in Jammu and Kashmir, where Pakistan-trained militants unleashed violence. Unlike the global norm, India does not have any fencing along the Line of Control (LoC). Now, things have changed. India has forces capable of using ultra-modern firearms and sophisticated weaponry. The ‘Sunderji Doctrine’ is being followed in the Army now. The Bhagavad Gita and the modern leader Dr R Balasubramaniam spoke on The Inner Charioteer – Gita and the Modern Leader. He said that, as a doctor, he had served for over 30 years in tribal areas. India’s survival was because of the development of rural India. Now, most of us are glued to mobile phones, laptops and gaming apps, irrespective of age and gender. In the Mahabharata, Dushasana attempted to disrobe Draupadi in the royal court of Hastinapur, culminating in the war between the Pandavas and the Kauravas. Had this not happened, the Bhagavad Gita would not have come into existence. Krishna explained to Arjuna the essence of life, war, peace and much more. Why are we this way? title: JCCT-IV Hyderabad Meet Brings Together 13 States, 11 Agencies to Tackle Cybercrime
excerpt: HYDERABAD: Officers from 13 states and 11 central and institutional agencies joined a joint cybercrime coordination meeting hosted by the Telangana Cyber Security Bureau (TGCSB) and the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) in Hyderabad on Monday to strengthen action against organised, multi-state cybercrime networks. The Joint Cyber Crime Coordination Team (JCCT-IV), Hyderabad Region, was […]HYDERABAD: Officers from 13 states and 11 central and institutional agencies joined a joint cybercrime coordination meeting hosted by the Telangana Cyber Security Bureau (TGCSB) and the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) in Hyderabad on Monday to strengthen action against organised, multi-state cybercrime networks. The Joint Cyber Crime Coordination Team (JCCT-IV), Hyderabad Region, was held at the Telangana Cyber Security Coordination Centre (TGiCCC) on November 3. The meeting brought together 45 officers from 13 other state law enforcement agencies, representatives of 11 central and institutional stakeholders, and police personnel from Telangana. The participating states were Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Delhi, Goa, Gujarat, Jharkhand, Karnataka, Kerala, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal. The agencies represented included I4C, CERT-In, National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB), Bureau of Police Research and Development (BPR&D), Reserve Bank of India (RBI), Enforcement Directorate (ED), Department of Telecommunications (DoT), Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), Intelligence Bureau (IB), National Forensic Sciences University (NFSU) and Telangana's Information Technology, Electronics and Communications Department. DGP calls for shifting focus from recovery to prevention Telangana Director General of Police C V Anand inaugurated the meeting. Principal Secretary to the Home Department and TGCSB director Shikha Goel outlined the agenda, while I4C chief executive officer Rajesh Kumar presented an overview of the national cybercrime situation. Anand said Telangana had been ranked first in the last two reviews by the Prime Minister's Office. He said cybercrime complaints increased by 24% across India in 2024-25, while Telangana recorded a 3% decline. Financial losses in the state fell by 20%, compared with a 4% reduction nationally, he said. "Cybercrime is now an organised industry, and we must shift from recovering money at the end of the chain to preventing the crime itself — denying criminals a target, a channel to reach the victim, a phone number and a usable account," Anand said. He expressed hope that the recommendations emerging from the meeting would be taken to the Centre for coordinated action across the country. Officials seek intelligence-led multi-state investigations Goel said cybercrime had evolved into an organised transnational ecosystem, with masterminds and financiers often remaining beyond the reach of investigators even after scam centres were dismantled and bank accounts blocked. "Criminals work as one network, we are constrained by jurisdictions," she said, calling for a shift from case-based investigations to intelligence-led coordination, real-time information sharing and joint operations across states. Rajesh Kumar said scam compounds were moving from Southeast Asia to Africa, Sri Lanka and other locations. He said all states except one had notified their State Cyber Crime Coordination Centres (S4Cs). He also referred to the Supreme Court's hearing on digital arrests and said it provided an opportunity for states to place their concerns before the court. Kumar outlined proposed second-generation reforms, including a unified investigation platform, a standard operating procedure for banks to enable them to stop suspicious transactions, and special nationwide operations targeting cybercrime infrastructure. Discussions focus on AI, mule accounts and online safety The sessions covered cybercrime prevention, inter-state investigation challenges, coordination with the Ministry of Home Affairs, investigation platforms, online crimes against women and children, and the legal framework and accountability surrounding artificial intelligence. Cyber law expert Pavan Duggal addressed the legal aspects of AI. Officials also discussed AI-enabled detection methods and shared practices from Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Karnataka and Telangana. The deliberations focused on strengthening nodal officer networks and escalation protocols, improving the use of I4C platforms, and developing preventive measures involving banks, telecom operators and digital platforms. The recommendations were consolidated by the TGCSB director and will be circulated among participating states and agencies for follow-up. Seven JCCTs are currently operating across the country, with centres at Mewat, Jamtara, Ahmedabad, Hyderabad, Chandigarh, Visakhapatnam and Guwahati. ]]>

title: MoS Margherita discusses India's Caribbean ties with ACS chief in Madrid
excerpt: Minister of State (MoS) for External Affairs Pabitra Margherita on Tuesday met Noemi Espinoza Madrid, Secretary General of the Association of Caribbean States (ACS), in Madrid and discussed India's engagement with the Global South, particularly in the Greater Caribbean region."Pleased to meet Noemi Espinoza Madrid, Secretary General of the Association of Caribbean States (ACS), in Madrid. Our conversation focused on India's engagement with the Global South, particularly in the Greater Caribbean region," Margherita said on social media platform X.Earlier in the day, the MoS had met business representatives from Spain's textile and tourism sectors to discuss ways to deepen bilateral cooperation."Interacted with business representatives from Spain's textile & tourism sectors. Discussed opportunities to strengthen India-Spain cooperation in textile trade, sourcing, manufacturing, sustainable textiles, investment and tourism, while also highlighting the importance of enhancing people-to-people ties," he said. Margherita also offered floral tributes at the statue of Mahatma Gandhi in Madrid on Tuesday, stressing the Mahatma's commitment to truth and non-violence as a guide for peace and harmony."Gandhiji's timeless ideals of truth and Ahimsa continue to inspire humanity," the MoS had said in a post on X.Margherita arrived in Madrid on Monday to attend the 30th Ibero-American Conference Summit, where India is set to join the Conference as an Associate Observer. The Conference has 22 member countries, along with 12 Associate Observers and 20 Consultative Observers. According to the Ministry of External Affairs, the visit will continue until November 5. During his stay, the MoS is expected to hold bilateral meetings with key counterparts on the sidelines of the summit and engage with the Indian community in Madrid. The Ministry has said the visit marks a milestone in the ongoing India-Spain Dual Year of Culture, Tourism and Artificial Intelligence celebrations.

title: Western Ghats Lit Fest 2026 | Day 2: Speakers explore Bharat’s civilisational heritage and challenges
excerpt: Coimbatore: The second day of the fifth edition of the Western Ghats Lit Fest 2026, held on October 25, witnessed discussions on the status of Hindus in Bharat, religious discrimination, temple administration, India’s maritime heritage, national security, economic thought, inner science and the country’s civilisational legacy. Speakers also examined ideological narratives, the Naxal movement, cow protection and the importance of preserving India’s cultural and literary traditions. The day began with prayers and the lighting of the ceremonial lamp, followed by an invocation by Sree Raja Durga. Anand Ranganathan questions discrimination against Hindus In his keynote address on Status of Hindus in the State of Bharat, author and commentator Dr Anand Ranganathan spoke about what he described as discrimination against Hindus, unequal treatment of religious institutions and the need for a change in policy. He said, “It is not a question of being second-class or third-class citizens. I thought things would possibly get better in the years to come. I am afraid that things have either got worse or remained the same. The Hindu candle, metaphorically speaking, is burning at both ends. If it were burning at only one end, we could possibly manage the situation or salvage something for a few more years. But the problem is that it is burning at both ends.” He argued that appeasement was being extended to all communities except Hindus and that differential treatment existed even within the Hindu community. He said the problem arose when appeasement crossed the boundary into discrimination. Referring to religious conversions, he said conversions through coercion, force or inducement were a different matter. Ranganathan also questioned what he described as a new phenomenon of Hindus celebrating conversions away from Hinduism. He said there was no objection to individuals choosing another religion, but questioned the attitude of those celebrating the departure of others from their religious tradition. He referred to instances of political leaders celebrating such conversions. Government control of Hindu temples Questioning the state control of Hindu temples, Ranganathan asked why Hindu temples alone were subjected to government control while mosques and gurdwaras were not governed by comparable arrangements. He questioned why a practice inherited from the British period continued after Independence and why the relevant constitutional and legal concerns had been overlooked when the Congress government introduced endowment laws in the 1950s. He said thousands of Hindu temples had subsequently come under government control. According to him, more than one lakh Hindu temples were under government control, leaving their administration vulnerable to the decisions of those in power. He alleged that temple funds could be diverted, temple lands taken over and institutions that had sustained Hindu religious and cultural life for centuries placed at the mercy of governments. Also Read: Western Ghats Lit Fest 2026 | Day 1: National security, heritage, Indic knowledge and Hindu identity take centre stage He cited Tamil Nadu as an example, stating that nearly 40,000 temples were under government control. Karnataka had a comparable number, approximately 35,000 to 36,000, he said. In Andhra Pradesh, he referred to laws and administrative practices that imposed financial obligations on prominent temples, including Tirupati. He questioned the practice of directing temple funds towards government projects such as flyovers and meeting administrative expenses, including audits. Referring to Keralam, he said the Communist establishment, despite describing religion as the opium of the masses, had exercised control over thousands of temples through various boards. He also referred to the difficulties faced by Sabarimala pilgrims, alleging that devotees had been packed together like sardines, with some reportedly suffocating and dying. Agama temples and Tamil Nadu’s temple administration Ranganathan criticised the Tamil Nadu government’s move concerning the classification of Agama temples as non-Agama temples. He referred to the figure of 30,000 out of the 40,000 temples under the Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments (HR&CE) Department. He described the development as disastrous, arguing that Agama temples had functioned according to established traditions for centuries, with priests performing specific duties passed down through generations. He said, “Suddenly, an administrator arrives and declares that the temple is no longer an Agama temple. According to the figures I have cited, this has happened to 25,000 temples.” He alleged that decisions detrimental to Hindu interests taken by the previous DMK government were being continued by the present government. Referring to the Thiruparankundram Karthigai Deepam issue, he said the TVK government had approached the Supreme Court in the matter and had not withdrawn its position despite judicial criticism of the earlier government’s actions. He also referred to the parole granted to individuals convicted in connection with the Coimbatore bombings, despite the Supreme Court having indicated that bail should be denied to them. He said parole had been granted to five associates of the mastermind Basha, who died approximately a year earlier. He also criticised the permission given for a procession through the same roads during Basha’s funeral, which drew thousands of Muslims. ‘Apply the same rules to mosques and churches’ Arguing that Hindus needed to recalibrate their demands, Ranganathan said that if the government maintained that existing laws governing Hindu institutions were not discriminatory, comparable rules should be applied to other religious institutions. He said Hindus should stop merely asking the state to relinquish control over temples and instead demand that the state take control of mosques and churches as well. “If the state can interfere in one community’s religious institutions, why should it not interfere in those belonging to other communities?” he asked, arguing that the government would probably relinquish control over Hindu temples within 24 hours if such a demand were made. He questioned the logic of government takeovers in the name of preventing corruption, asking whether corruption in any organisation justified its takeover by the state. He also questioned how a government frequently accused of corruption could be considered the appropriate institution to eliminate corruption in religious bodies. He said the Congress was responsible for introducing several of the laws, but questioned why the present government continued to implement them. Places of Worship Act and […]

title: Industry-academia gap needs to be bridged to prepare youth for 2047: Gujarat CM
excerpt: Gandhinagar, Nov 3 (IANS) Gujarat Chief Minister Bhupendra Patel has called for closer coordination between educational institutions and industries to prepare young people for the changing demands of the job market, saying the state's competitiveness by 2047 would depend on the quality of education and skills imparted to its youth. Addressing the valedictory session of a one-day conference on ‘Viksit Gujarat@2047: Higher Education for Future Workforce Readiness’ in Ahmedabad on Tuesday, Patel said developing a skilled talent pool and strengthening youth employability must be central to the state's roadmap for "Viksit Gujarat 2047", which is aligned with the national vision of "Viksit Bharat 2047". The conference was organised by the Gujarat State Institution for Transformation (GRIT) in collaboration with the state government's Higher Education Department. Describing the initiative as "timely", Patel said future-oriented education and preparedness were essential to empowering young people. Custom Ad: Multiplex He said the state government's roadmap should be implemented with an open approach, taking into account suggestions and cooperation from all stakeholders to ensure result-oriented outcomes. "The government is flexible in implementing this roadmap and remains open to adopting suitable approaches based on valuable suggestions from stakeholders," he said. Patel said today's youth would form an important part of the workforce needed to realise the vision of Viksit Gujarat and Viksit Bharat by 2047. "Their development through relevant education and skills suited to changing requirements would determine Gujarat's competitiveness in the coming years," he added. He also suggested that similar seminars and discussions be organised every three or six months to review progress and provide a clear direction to the state's development roadmap. The outcomes of the discussions at the conference, he said, would help advance efforts towards achieving the 2047 goals. Referring to India's progress under Prime Minister Narendra Modi's leadership, Patel said: "The country had emerged as a powerful nation and was advancing rapidly on the global stage." Minister of State for Higher and Technical Education, Trikam Chhanga, who also attended the event, stressed the need to promote digital literacy and technology-based education across academic disciplines. "Students should be equipped to use emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, data analytics, semiconductor manufacturing, electronics and automation, irrespective of their fields of study," he said. Chhanga said universities should regularly revise their curricula in collaboration with industries in line with the multidisciplinary and experiential learning approach of the 'National Education Policy-2020'. He also called for greater emphasis on internships and research to improve students' practical exposure and employability. He said coordinated efforts were needed to equip young people with skills suited to the requirements of the local economy, particularly in sectors such as manufacturing, agriculture, the marine industry, tourism and logistics. During the conference, NITI Aayog Programme Director Dr Sonia Pant delivered a presentation on ‘Higher Education for Viksit Bharat’, highlighting the need for a higher education system aligned with future workforce requirements, skill development and employment-oriented learning. Discussions at the conference focused on aligning higher education with emerging employment needs, strengthening partnerships between educational institutions and industries, and expanding skill development opportunities. --IANS mys/dan

title: Gujarat govt eyes bigger share of markets under India's FTAs
excerpt: Gujarat, which accounts for nearly a quarter of India's merchandise exports, could gain access to a combined import market of more than USD 1.08 trillion across India's Free Trade Agreement (FTA) partner countries, with the state government set to highlight export opportunities at the 'Vibrant Gujarat Global Summit 2027' in January. The three-day summit, scheduled to be held at Mahatma Mandir in Gandhinagar from January 10 to 12, will feature dedicated sectoral sessions on India's expanding network of trade agreements and their potential to strengthen the state's industrial and export base. India currently has nine FTAs involving 38 countries, providing preferential access to international markets for domestic manufacturers and service providers. Gujarat already exports goods worth USD 37.8 billion to FTA partner countries, accounting for nearly 34 per cent of its total merchandise exports. The state exported merchandise worth USD 110.6 billion in the financial year 2025-26, making it India's largest exporting state. Its merchandise exports more than doubled from Rs 4.44 lakh crore in 2013-14 to Rs 9.77 lakh crore in 2025-26. The opportunities are spread across several sectors in which Gujarat has an established industrial presence, including chemicals and petrochemicals, marine products, agro-processed foods, gems and jewellery, textiles and apparel, engineering and automobiles. The state's traditional AYUSH wellness sector, along with digital services and artificial intelligence, could also benefit from greater access to international markets. Across major FTA partner markets, the combined import demand for sectors relevant to Gujarat exceeds USD 1.08 trillion, offering considerable scope for expanding exports and diversifying trade destinations. India's FTA network has expanded through a series of agreements over the past five years. These include the Comprehensive Economic Cooperation and Partnership Agreement with Mauritius, signed in February 2021; the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement with the UAE in February 2022; and the Economic Cooperation and Trade Agreement with Australia in April 2022. India subsequently signed the Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement with the four-member European Free Trade Association (EFTA), comprising Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein, in March 2024. This was followed by the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement with the United Kingdom in July 2025 and the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement with Oman in December 2025. Negotiations for a trade agreement with the European Union concluded in January 2026, while an FTA with New Zealand was signed in April 2026. India's growing export base has provided further momentum to these trade initiatives. The country's combined merchandise and services exports reached a record USD 863.1 billion in FY 2025-26, including merchandise exports of USD 441.8 billion. During April-June 2026, combined exports were estimated at USD 232.73 billion, an increase of 11.37 per cent over the corresponding period of the previous year. The agreements are also expected to create opportunities for entrepreneurs and women-led micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), particularly in textiles, leather goods and handicrafts, by improving their access to overseas markets and making their products more competitive. Unlike traditional trade arrangements focused primarily on reducing tariffs, newer-generation FTAs also cover areas such as digital trade, mobility, sustainability, innovation and regulatory cooperation. Their effective implementation and utilisation, along with export diversification, will be important in ensuring that businesses, including smaller enterprises, can benefit from preferential market access. The state government plans to use the 'Vibrant Gujarat Global Summit' and its associated events to connect international markets with the state's industrial clusters and explore opportunities for investment, trade partnerships and collaboration. Aligning the agreements with district-level industrial strengths and sector-specific capabilities is expected to help Gujarat expand its role in global manufacturing and supply chains. The initiative is also being positioned within India's broader ambition of achieving the goal of 'Viksit Bharat @2047', with the state seeking to strengthen its contribution to the country's next phase of export-led growth.
